blocks.text:
Design a Tic-Tac-Toe Game for two players on an N by N board (classically 3x3). Players alternate placing their symbol, X or O, and the first to complete an entire row, column, or diagonal wins. If the board fills up with no winner, the game is a draw.

  • Actors: two players, X and O, alternating turns.
  • Scope: a configurable N by N board, win detection across rows, columns and both diagonals.
  • Goal: detect a win the instant it genuinely happens, without ever rescanning the entire board on every move.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: a move is only accepted on an empty, in-bounds cell, and a win is detected the instant the placed mark completes a full row, column, or diagonal. Everything else builds on top of that.

items: The system shall support two players alternating turns on an N by N board.
The system shall reject a move on a cell that is already occupied or outside the board.
The system shall detect a win the moment a row, column, or diagonal is fully completed by one symbol.
The system shall detect a draw once the board is completely full with no winner.
The system shall notify listeners of every move, every win, and every draw.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: correctness, generality, observability and efficiency

items: Correctness: a win must be detected the instant it truly happens, never a move late or early.
Generality: the win-checking design should work for any board size, not be hardcoded to 3x3.
Observability: every move, win, and draw must be visible to anything watching the game.
Efficiency: checking for a win after a move should only examine the row, column, and diagonal that move actually touches, never the whole board.
Thread Safety: two rapid move submissions must never corrupt whose turn it actually is.
Should the board size be fixed at 3x3, or configurable to any N by N size?
Is a draw simply "board full with no winner," or are there other draw conditions to consider?
Do we need to support more than two players, or exactly two, X and O?
Should move history be tracked for replay or undo functionality?
Do we need built-in support for an AI opponent, or is this strictly a two-human-player design?
The board size is configurable at game creation time, the classic case is 3x3 but the design generalizes to any N.
Exactly two players alternate turns, in the order they were registered.
A draw is defined strictly as the board being completely full with no winning line.
No AI opponent is implemented, both players submit moves through the same makeMove() API.
Move history persistence is out of scope for the core game loop, a database design is still covered separately.

metadata.alt: TicTacToeGame composing a Board, Players, a list of WinningStrategy checks, and notifying GameListeners

items: Symbol: the three possible cell states, EMPTY, X, or O.
Board: the N by N grid, plus the ability to place a mark and check fullness.
WinningStrategy: one specific way of winning (a row, a column, or a diagonal) that can be checked after any move.
Player: a name and an assigned symbol.
GameListener: anything that wants to react to a move, a win, or a draw.
TicTacToeGame: the orchestrator tying turns, moves, win checks and events together.

metadata.alt: TicTacToeGame composing the Board and managing both Player instances

items: Composition: TicTacToeGame composes its Board, the board has no purpose outside the specific game session that owns it.
Aggregation: the game aggregates its list of WinningStrategy instances, the exact same strategies could be reused across a fresh game.
Association: the game is associated with its Player list and any GameListeners, both configurable independently of the game’s own core logic.
Realization: RowWinStrategy, ColumnWinStrategy and DiagonalWinStrategy each realize WinningStrategy; ConsoleGameListener realizes GameListener.

metadata.alt: TicTacToeGame tying together Board, WinningStrategy implementations, Player and GameListener

blocks.text: Notice that TicTacToeGame never contains any win-checking logic itself, it simply asks each registered WinningStrategy whether the just-placed move won. This is exactly what section 9 covers next.
Three patterns keep this design efficient, correct, and genuinely extensible.

metadata.alt: RowWinStrategy, ColumnWinStrategy and DiagonalWinStrategy all implementing the shared WinningStrategy contract

blocks.text: Why needed: a win can happen three structurally different ways, a full row, a full column, or a full diagonal, and checking all three naively means rescanning the whole board every single move. Why best: each strategy only examines the specific line the last move actually touched, and TicTacToeGame never needs to know the details of how any one check works. What it solves: keeps win-checking both efficient (only the relevant line is checked) and independently extensible (a future "both diagonals must match" variant is just one more strategy).

metadata.alt: TicTacToeGame notifying every registered GameListener of moves, wins and draws

blocks.text: Why needed: a console UI, a web UI, and a scoreboard tracker might all want to react to the same moves and outcomes, without the game itself needing to know any of them exist. Why best: new listener types can be added freely with zero changes to TicTacToeGame’s core logic. What it solves: keeps event reporting fully decoupled from the actual game rules.

metadata.alt: PlayerFactory turning a plain text symbol into a validated Player instance

blocks.text: Why needed: creating a Player from raw input (like a symbol typed by a user or read from configuration) needs validation that the symbol is actually X or O. Why best: centralizing this check in PlayerFactory means Player itself can trust it always holds a valid symbol. What it solves: keeps invalid-symbol handling in exactly one place instead of scattered wherever a Player might be constructed.

items: Board: responsibility is owning the grid and answering placement and fullness questions. Attributes: grid, size. Methods: placeMark(), getCell(), getSize(), isFull().
RowWinStrategy / ColumnWinStrategy / DiagonalWinStrategy: responsibility is checking exactly one line type for a completed win. Methods: checkWin() (each implemented differently).
Player: responsibility is holding a name and a fixed symbol. Attributes: name, symbol.

TicTacToeGame: responsibility is coordinating turns, moves, win detection, and draw detection. Attributes: board, players, currentPlayerIndex, winningStrategies, listeners, gameOver. Methods: makeMove(), addListener().

metadata.alt: WinningStrategy and GameListener as the two extension points, each with one concrete implementation shown

blocks.text: WinningStrategy isolates how a specific line type is checked, letting new win conditions be added without touching TicTacToeGame. GameListener isolates reactions to game events, letting any number of independent observers watch the same game.
Three workflows matter most: a move that does not win, a move that does win, and a move that ends in a draw.

metadata.alt: A move placed successfully, with no WinningStrategy reporting a win, so the turn simply passes along

blocks.text: This is the routine case, the move is validated, placed, listeners are told about it, every strategy is checked, none report a win, and play continues.

metadata.alt: A move that completes an entire row, detected by RowWinStrategy, ending the game

blocks.text: Only the strategy relevant to the completed line needs to report true, the moment any one strategy does, the game ends immediately, no further strategies need to be checked.

metadata.alt: The final cell being filled with no strategy reporting a win, resolved as a draw

blocks.text: A draw is only ever checked after every winning strategy has already reported false, a full board is never itself sufficient to end the game if a winning line exists.

metadata.alt: The full turn sequence: bounds and occupancy check, placement, win check, draw check, then the next turn

items: Happy path, plain move: the move is valid, placed, does not complete a line, and the board is not yet full, so the turn passes to the other player.
Happy path, winning move: the move completes a row, column, or diagonal, the game ends immediately with that player as the winner.
Happy path, draw: the move fills the last empty cell without completing any line, the game ends in a draw.
Failure, invalid move: the requested cell is out of bounds or already occupied, the move is rejected and the board is left completely unchanged.
TicTacToeGame.makeMove(int row, int col): the single entry point for attempting a move, returns whether the game ended as a result.
TicTacToeGame.addListener(GameListener): registers a new observer for game events.
Board.isFull(): the core query draw detection is built on.
WinningStrategy.checkWin(Board, row, col, symbol): the contract every win-checking rule must implement.

metadata.alt: A move on an occupied or out of range cell being rejected, leaving the board completely unchanged

items: Invalid input: a move with a row or column outside the board’s range is rejected before any grid access is attempted.
Resource unavailable: not directly applicable to the in-memory version, a persisted variant would need to handle a failed save gracefully.
Business-rule violation: PlayerFactory.createPlayer() throws immediately on an unrecognized symbol, rather than silently creating an invalid player.
System failure: a broken game listener throwing an exception should be caught per-listener, not allowed to prevent the move itself from being correctly applied.

metadata.alt: Two near-simultaneous move submissions both needing to safely read and update the shared board and turn state

blocks.text: makeMove() reads and writes the shared Board grid and currentPlayerIndex together, if two move requests are processed concurrently, the turn-check and the actual placement can interleave incorrectly, potentially letting both players move out of turn. The entire makeMove() call must be synchronized around a single lock, exactly as with the earlier problems in this series.

items: Supporting a larger board (say 5x5 requiring 4 in a row to win) requires only a different WinningStrategy set, zero changes to TicTacToeGame’s core loop.
Supporting more than two players is mostly already handled by the players list and modulo turn advancement, the main change would be relaxing assumptions about exactly two symbols.
Adding a ScoreboardListener that tracks win counts across many games is a pure GameListener implementation, no core changes needed.
Future work: adding an AI opponent would sit as a new "player" that computes its own move and calls makeMove(), the same entry point a human uses.
Single Responsibility: Board only manages the grid, each WinningStrategy only checks one line type, TicTacToeGame only orchestrates turns.
Open/Closed: new winning conditions and listener types can be added without modifying TicTacToeGame’s existing, already-correct logic.
Liskov Substitution: any WinningStrategy or GameListener implementation can be substituted freely without TicTacToeGame needing to know which one it has.
Interface Segregation: WinningStrategy exposes exactly one method, GameListener exposes exactly the three events it genuinely needs.
Dependency Inversion: TicTacToeGame depends on the WinningStrategy and GameListener abstractions, never on a specific concrete implementation.
A move on the very last empty cell that also happens to complete a line: the win must be reported, not a draw, win detection always runs before the fullness check.
A 1x1 board (a degenerate case): the very first move immediately satisfies every winning strategy simultaneously.
A player attempting to move twice in a row: rejected implicitly, since makeMove() always uses whichever player currentPlayerIndex currently points to.

Two diagonal wins completing on the exact same move (only possible at the exact center of an odd-sized board): DiagonalWinStrategy already checks both diagonals independently and reports a win if either matches.
Board.placeMark() / getCell(): O(1), direct array indexing.
RowWinStrategy / ColumnWinStrategy: O(N) where N is the board size, scanning exactly one line.
DiagonalWinStrategy: O(N) as well, scanning at most two diagonals of length N.
makeMove(): O(N) overall, dominated by the winning strategy checks, never O(N squared) since the whole board is never rescanned.
Space: O(N squared) for the board itself, O(1) additional space per move.

metadata.alt: GAME tracking its PLAYER rows and a full MOVE history for replay and analysis

blocks.text: Persisting completed games is straightforward: GAME stores the board size and final status, PLAYER links each symbol to a real user, and MOVE records the full move sequence in order, enough to reconstruct and replay any game exactly as it was played.

items: How would you generalize this design to require exactly K in a row on a board larger than K by K, like Gomoku?
How would you add an AI opponent, and where would that decision-making logic plug into this design?
How would you support undo, letting a player take back their last move?
How would you test that win detection is correct for every possible winning line on a large N by N board without manually enumerating each one?

items: Why check only the row, column and diagonal touched by the LAST move, instead of scanning the whole board after every move? Because a move can only ever complete a line that passes through the cell it was just placed on, scanning anywhere else is wasted work.

Why does DiagonalWinStrategy check "is this cell even on a diagonal" before doing any real work? Because most cells on a board larger than 3x3 are not on either diagonal at all, this short-circuit avoids unnecessary scanning on the common case.

Why is PlayerFactory a separate class rather than validation logic inside Player’s constructor directly? Both are defensible, but keeping it separate lets Player stay a pure data holder, and lets future creation logic (like assigning symbols automatically) live in one dedicated place.

An alternative could maintain running counters per row, column and diagonal (incremented or decremented as marks are placed) for true O(1) win checking, faster, but noticeably more bookkeeping and harder to read for a teaching-oriented design.

A simpler design could just rescan the entire board after every move, easier to write correctly, but wastes work proportional to the whole board size on every single move instead of just the relevant line.

Supporting arbitrary "K in a row" win conditions (not just full lines) would require a more general sliding-window check inside each strategy, a reasonable extension but out of scope for classic Tic-Tac-Toe.
Persist the move history (already modeled via the MOVE table) so games can be resumed or replayed after a disconnect.
Validate every move server-side even if a client also validates locally, never trust a client to enforce game rules.
Add rate limiting on move submission per player to prevent a buggy or malicious client from flooding makeMove() calls.
Expose a read-only board snapshot API separately from makeMove(), so spectators or replay tooling never risk mutating game state.
